transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, hello Dr. ____. Nice to meet you, I guess. So, what brings me in... well, I work as a personal care aide. Have for a while now. And we have these mandatory staff meetings, usually Tuesday mornings, where we just sit around the breakroom drinking bad coffee and talking about protocols and state regulations and all that stuff. Now, fall prevention is a massive deal in our line of work. I mean, one slip and you've got a broken hip, endless incident reports, and a poor senior in the hospital, right? It's serious business. 

So anyway, we were in this meeting, and they brought up the fall-prevention guidelines, and I don't know, I just... I got really, really worked up about it. I felt this rush, and I had to show them, not just tell them. I got up and started acting out the whole fall-prevention drill right there in the middle of the room. I was grabbing the folding chairs—you know those heavy metal ones that scrape real loud on the linoleum?—and I was moving them all around, waving my arms everywhere to demonstrate exactly how you're supposed to block a fall and guide somebody down safely. 

And the thing is, I was just so into it, I couldn't seem to stop. My supervisor and the other folks, they were staring at me, and they kept telling me, "Okay, we get the point, you can sit down now," but I just kept going with the chairs and the arm waving. I couldn't stop even when they were outright demanding I sit down, I just had to finish showing the whole procedure. So... I guess that's why my boss told me I needed to come see a doctor today.
Around that time, were you feeling unusually energized or ‘amped up’ in a way that lasted for several days?

Yeah, I guess you could say that. It's like... well, there are these stretches, right? Days at a time where I just wake up and I feel so incredibly bright and fired up. It’s this feeling like everything is finally lining up, you know? Like the whole world makes sense and I’ve got the energy to tackle every single thing on my plate, and then some. I'll be buzzing around the facility, getting all my patients sorted, organizing the supply closet even though nobody asked me to, just feeling completely unstoppable. 

But the flip side of that—and this is what gets me into trouble, I think—is that if someone tries to slow me down when I'm in that zone, or if they question what I'm doing, I just... I snap. I snap so much harder than I mean to. Like during that meeting, when my supervisor was telling me to sit down? I felt this intense spike of anger, just pure irritation, because in my head I was doing this incredibly important thing and they were just being obstacles. It’s like I have all this electricity running through me, and it feels great until someone gets in the way of the current, and then it just sparks out and burns whoever is standing closest. It's not that I want to be mean, it's just... I can't handle the friction when I'm moving that fast.
During those energized stretches, do you ever feel unusually important, powerful, or like you have special abilities?

Well, "special abilities" might be pushing it, but... I do get this overwhelming, undeniable sense that I just *know* things. Like, I understand safety protocols and how to genuinely care for these older folks on a level that nobody else does. Especially not the people sitting in the offices with the fancy titles and the degrees, you know? The administrators who just look at spreadsheets all day. 

When I'm in one of those stretches, it’s like... it’s like my eyes are completely open to how the whole system is flawed, and I’m the only one who can see the matrix of it all. I look around the senior center and I see a hundred different things that need fixing—the way the rugs are laid out, the timing of the medication rounds, how the grab bars are positioned in the showers—and I just know, I absolutely know, that if they would just put me in charge, if they would just listen to me and let me implement my ideas, I could fix the entire facility. 

It feels like a calling, almost. Like I was specifically chosen or put there in that exact job to revolutionize how we do personal care. I start thinking, "Why am I just an aide when I clearly have the vision to run this whole place?" And that’s why I get so frustrated when they tell me to sit down or follow the standard handbook. Because in those moments, I feel like I'm operating on this totally different, higher frequency than them, and they’re just holding back progress by not recognizing what I bring to the table. I mean, they just don't see the big picture the way I do when I'm feeling like that.
During those energized stretches, do you need much less sleep than usual and still feel rested?

Yeah, actually, that's a huge part of it. It’s funny you ask that because, normally, I'm the kind of guy who needs a solid seven or eight hours, you know? If I don't get it, I'm dragging. But when I'm in one of those zones, when the electricity is just humming through me... sleep just feels like this massive waste of time. I mean, who wants to lie there unconscious when there's so much to figure out and so much to do? 

I'll go to bed at maybe midnight, maybe one in the morning, and then—boom—it's three a.m. or maybe four, and my eyes just pop open. And I'm not groggy. I'm not hitting the snooze button or rolling over. I am wide awake, completely refreshed, like I just slept for ten hours. I can sleep two or three hours, wake up before dawn feeling totally ready to go, and not think anything is wrong with being up making plans while the house is still dark. 

I'll be sitting at my kitchen table with a notepad, just sketching out new shift schedules for the aides, or writing down lists of safety hazards I noticed the day before. The house is completely silent, pitch black outside, and I'm just sitting there, totally wired, thinking, "This is the best time of day, this is when the real work gets done." And I'll go through my whole shift that next day, lifting patients, doing the rounds, and I won't even yawn once. It’s like my body just decides it doesn't need to recharge the normal way anymore. It just runs on whatever that energy is. And honestly, it feels great at the time, even if it probably sounds a little crazy now. I just get so much done when everyone else is sleeping.
Before these energetic periods ever started, have you generally been very shy or held back in social situations because you worry about being criticized or rejected?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, sure, everybody gets a little nervous sometimes, right? Like if you're meeting your girlfriend's parents for the first time or going into a big job interview—which, honestly, I haven't had to do in a while because I've been at the center for a bit now. But generally speaking? No, I'm not a shy guy. I've never been the type to just sit in the corner and worry about what people are thinking of me. 

Actually, it's usually the opposite. I'm the one who's always talking to the residents, joking around with the nurses, making sure everybody's having a good time. I like being around people. I mean, you kind of have to be a people person to do what I do, right? You're helping folks with some really personal, intimate stuff—bathing, getting dressed, moving from the bed to the chair—and if you're awkward or worried about them judging you, it just makes the whole thing uncomfortable for everyone. So, no, I've always been pretty outgoing. I don't really hold back or bite my tongue because I'm scared somebody's going to criticize me. If they do, they do, you know? I just brush it off. I’ve always been pretty confident in who I am and what I’m doing, even before all this... electricity stuff started happening. I just don't have time to sit around worrying if people like me or not.
Have these attention-seeking or dramatic behaviors been part of your personality for as long as you can remember, or do they only happen during these energized periods?

Well, I wouldn't really call it attention-seeking, to be honest. I mean, I know how it probably looks to the administration when I'm in there trying to reorganize the whole dining room layout during the lunch rush, but it's not like I'm doing it to get people to look at me. I'm doing it because it needs to be done! 

But, uh, to answer your question... no, I haven't always been like that. Like I said, I've always been outgoing, sure. I like to joke with the residents, maybe do a little dance when the radio's on in the rec room just to get a smile out of Mr. Henderson—he's this grumpy old guy in room 204, but I know how to make him laugh. But that's just being friendly, you know? That's just having a good bedside manner. 

This other stuff... the feeling like I need to take charge, the talking really fast, the feeling like I have to explain my grand vision for the facility to anyone who will listen... that only really happens when I'm in one of those zones. When that energy is just pushing me forward. If I'm not in one of those stretches, I'm just a regular guy doing my job. I punch in, I do my rounds, I chat with the folks, I punch out. I don't feel this... this burning need to be the center of everything or to revolutionize the place. It's only when the electricity hits that I get so, I guess you could say, intense about everything. It's like a switch flips, and suddenly I'm not just an aide anymore, I'm the guy who has to fix the whole world, starting with the senior center. But normally? No, normally I'm just me.
During these energized periods, do you ever do things that are clearly out of character or risky, like spending a lot of money, reckless driving, or sexual behavior you normally wouldn't do?

Well, risky... I mean, I don't know if I'd call it risky, but I guess other people might? I haven't really noticed myself doing anything crazy like blowing my entire paycheck at the casino or driving my truck into a ditch, you know? I'm not out there racing cars down the highway or anything like that. But, um... I don't know, maybe I'm not the best judge of it when I'm in that headspace. 

Like, I don't go out and buy a new car or empty my bank account. I'm pretty careful with my money, usually, because, let's face it, being an aide doesn't exactly make you a millionaire. But when that energy is going, I might just... I don't know, I might go to the hardware store and buy a bunch of supplies to build a new ramp for the back entrance of the center, even though nobody asked me to and I definitely don't have the budget for it. But I just feel like, "This has to happen right now, and I'm the only one who sees it." But as far as like, reckless driving or, you know, going out and sleeping around... no, I haven't noticed anything like that. I just get really, really focused on my ideas. So, no, I wouldn't say I do those kinds of risky things you're talking about. I'm just trying to get things done.
When these energized periods happen, how long do they usually last?

Well, it's not like it's just a day or two, you know? It's more of a... a whole thing. Like, these stretches where I'm just buzzing, where the electricity is so loud and I'm barely sleeping—maybe two hours a night, if that, and I wake up feeling like I could run a marathon—and I'm just pushing all these big plans for the center, trying to get everybody on board with my vision... it's been happening for a while now. I'd say, if I really think back on it, it's been coming and going for about 11 months. 

Yeah, almost a year of this back and forth. It started around the end of last summer, I remember because it was right around the time they were talking about repaving the parking lot at the center, and I just got so fired up about how they were doing it all wrong. I stayed up for three nights straight drawing up new blueprints for the traffic flow. And since then, it just kind of rolls in, takes over for a while, and then rolls back out. It's not every single day of the 11 months, but it's like a tide, you know? Sometimes I'm just me, doing my job, and then boom, the energy hits again and I'm off to the races, trying to fix everything in sight. It's exhausting when I look back on it, but when I'm in it, I just feel like there's not enough time in the day to do all the things I need to do.
